content: These centers have been recognized since the 1970s, but their frequency has decreased as the overall incidence of hepatitis A among children has declined in recent years. Infections among children are typically mild or asymptomatic, and outbreaks are often identified only when adult contacts, usually parents, become ill. Poor hygiene among children who wear diapers, as well as the handling and changing of diapers by staff, contribute to the spread of hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection. Outbreaks rarely occur in child care centers where care is provided exclusively to toilet-trained children. Although child care centers may have been the source of hepatitis A outbreaks in certain communities, the disease in these centers more commonly reflects extended transmission from the community. Despite outbreaks occurring when HAV is introduced into child care centers, serologic surveys do not indicate a substantially increased prevalence of HAV infection among staff at these centers compared to control populations. Nosocomial transmission of HAV in health-care institutions is rare. Outbreaks have occasionally been observed in neonatal intensive care units due to infants acquiring infection from transfused blood and subsequently transmitting hepatitis A to other infants and staff. Outbreaks of hepatitis A caused by transmission from adult patients to health-care workers are typically associated with fecal incontinence. However, most hospitalized patients with hepatitis A are admitted after the onset of jaundice, when they are beyond the peak period of infectivity. Data from serologic surveys of health-care workers have not shown an increased prevalence of HAV infection in these groups compared to control populations. Historically, HAV infection was highly endemic in institutions for persons with developmental disabilities. As fewer children have been institutionalized and as conditions in these institutions have improved, the incidence and prevalence of HAV infection have decreased, although outbreaks can still occur in these settings. In the United States, cases of hepatitis A in elementary or secondary schools typically reflect disease acquisition in the community. Child-to-child transmission of the disease in schools is uncommon. If multiple cases occur among children at a school, the possibility of a common source of infection should be investigated. Studies comparing wastewater workers to appropriate control populations have not identified a substantial or consistent increase in the prevalence of anti-HAV among wastewater workers. No work-related instances of HAV transmission have been reported among wastewater workers in the United States. With the availability of hepatitis A vaccines beginning in 1995, hepatitis A became a vaccine-preventable disease. The use of these highly effective vaccines provided an opportunity to protect individuals from infection, reduce disease incidence by preventing transmission, and ultimately eliminate indigenous HAV transmission. Soon after the introduction of hepatitis A vaccines in the United States, a strategy of routine vaccination of children was recognized as having the potential to achieve a sustained reduction in the overall incidence of hepatitis A. This was accomplished by preventing infection among age groups that accounted for at least one-third of cases and eliminating a major source of infection for others. However, hepatitis A vaccines could not be readily incorporated into the routine infant and early childhood immunization schedule because they were not licensed for children under 2 years of age. To address these logistical barriers, a novel vaccination strategy was developed based on the unique epidemiology of hepatitis A and insights from demonstration projects and other research. This strategy involved the incremental implementation of routine childhood hepatitis A vaccination. Initial recommendations primarily focused on vaccinating individuals in populations at increased risk for hepatitis A and, as the first step in the incremental strategy, vaccinating children living in communities with the highest disease rates. While vaccinating high-risk populations provided protection to these individuals, it had little effect on national disease rates because the majority of cases did not occur among these groups. Although routine vaccination of children in high-incidence communities effectively reduced disease rates in those areas, the impact on national disease incidence was limited because most nationally reported cases occurred outside these communities.
